input: is a lock basically a normal variable, and what states can it be in?
expected_output: A lock is just a variable that you declare, and it holds the state of the lock. It is either available (also called unlocked or free), meaning no thread holds it, or acquired (locked or held), meaning exactly one thread holds it and is presumably in a critical section.

evidence.quote: A lock is just a variable, and thus to use one, you must declare a lock variable of some kind (such as mutex above).
It is either available (or unlocked or free) and thus no thread holds the lock, or acquired (or locked or held), and thus exactly one thread holds the lock and presumably is in a critical section.
This lock variable (or just “lock” for short) holds the state of the lock at any instant in time.

input: whats it called when a lock spins for a bit and then sleeps if it cant get in?
expected_output: It is called a two-phase lock. Spinning can be useful, particularly if the lock is about to be released, so in the first phase the lock spins for a while hoping to acquire it. If that fails, a second phase begins in which the caller is put to sleep and only woken up when the lock becomes free later.

evidence.quote: A two-phase lock realizes that spinning can be useful, particularly if the lock is about to be released. So in the first phase, the lock spins for a while, hoping that it can acquire the lock.
if the lock is not acquired during the first spin phase, a second phase is entered, where the caller is put to sleep, and only woken up when the lock becomes free later.

input: lock spins while flag is 1 then sets it to 1, why can two threads still get in?
expected_output: Checking the variable and setting it are separate steps, so an unlucky interrupt can switch threads in between. Then both threads can get past the loop and both set the variable to 1, so both enter the critical section and mutual exclusion is broken.

evidence.quote: As you can see from this interleaving, with timely (untimely?) interrupts, we can easily produce a case where both threads set the flag to 1 and both threads are thus able to enter the critical section.
This behavior is what professionals call “bad” – we have obviously failed to provide the most basic requirement: providing mutual exclusion.

notes: master: applied strict-review fix | master: tone rewrite

input: how does an atomic swap instruction make a lock safe vs just reading then writing?
expected_output: This is the test-and-set (atomic exchange) instruction. It returns the old value at a memory location and simultaneously updates it to a new value, and this whole sequence is performed atomically. Because both the test of the old lock value and the set of the new value are one atomic operation, only one thread acquires the lock, unlike a separate read followed by a write, where another thread can slip in between.

evidence.quote: It returns the old value pointed to by the ptr, and simultaneously updates said value to new. The key, of course, is that this sequence of operations is performed atomically.
By making both the test (of the old lock value) and set (of the new value) a single atomic operation, we ensure that only one thread acquires the lock.
The simplest bit of hardware support to understand is what is known as a test-and-set instruction, also known as atomic exchange.

As you can see from this interleaving, with timely (untimely?) interrupts, we can easily produce a case where both threads set the flag to 1 and both threads are thus able to enter the critical section.

notes: master: applied strict-review fix | master: tone rewrite

input: On MIPS-style hardware, if two threads both read the lock as free before either one writes, how does the conditional write stop both of them from winning?
expected_output: Only one of the two threads will succeed in updating the flag to 1 and acquire the lock. The second thread to attempt the store-conditional fails, because the other thread updated the flag between its load-linked and its store-conditional, so it has to try to acquire the lock again.

evidence.quote: only one of these threads will succeed in updating the flag to 1 and thus acquire the lock;

the second thread to attempt the store-conditional will fail (because the other thread updated the value of flag between its load-linked and store-conditional) and thus have to try to acquire the lock again.

input: in the sleeping lock, why doesnt the unlocker set the flag back to 0 before waking someone?
expected_output: It is not an error but a necessity. A woken thread returns from park() without holding the guard, so it cannot even try to set the flag to 1. Instead the lock is passed directly from the releasing thread to the next acquiring thread, and the flag is not set to 0 in between.

evidence.quote: When a thread is woken up, it will be as if it is returning from park(); however, it does not hold the guard at that point in the code and thus cannot even try to set the flag to 1.
Thus, we just pass the lock directly from the thread releasing the lock to the next thread acquiring it; flag is not set to 0 in-between.
Why is this? Well, it is not an error, but rather a necessity!

input: does compare-and-swap beat test-and-set when all i want is a plain spin lock?
expected_output: Compare-and-swap is a more powerful instruction than test-and-set, but that does not help for this purpose. If you just build a simple spin lock with it, its behavior is identical to the test-and-set spin lock.

evidence.quote: compare-and-swap is a more powerful instruction than test-and-set.
However, if we just build a simple spin lock with it, its behavior is identical to the spin lock we analyzed above.

input: Why does busy-waiting hurt so much when all the threads share one processor, yet is mostly fine when every thread has its own core?
expected_output: On one CPU, if the lock holder is preempted, each other thread spins for a whole time slice before giving up the CPU, wasting cycles. With multiple CPUs, a waiter spins on its own processor while the holder runs on another, and since the critical section is presumably short, the lock soon becomes available and not many cycles are wasted.

evidence.quote: each of those threads will spin for the duration of a time slice before giving up the CPU, a waste of CPU cycles.

presumably the critical section is short, and thus soon the lock becomes available, and is acquired by Thread B. Spinning to wait for a lock held on another processor doesn’t waste many cycles in this case, and thus can be effective.
For spin locks, in the single CPU case, performance overheads can be quite painful; imagine the case where the thread holding the lock is pre-empted within a critical section.
However, on multiple CPUs, spin locks work reasonably well (if the number of threads roughly equals the number of CPUs).

input: 10 threads share one cpu and the one with my spin lock gets preempted, how many time slices get wasted spinning?
expected_output: With N threads contending, about N - 1 time slices can be wasted spinning, so with 10 threads that is 9 slices.

evidence.quote: The problem gets worse with N threads contending for a lock; N −1 time slices may be wasted in a similar manner, simply spinning and waiting for a single thread to release the lock.

input: ticket lock with both counters at 0, A B C call lock in order, what number does each get, who goes after A unlocks?
expected_output: Each thread does an atomic fetch-and-add on the ticket value, which returns the old value and bumps it by one, so A gets 0, B gets 1 and C gets 2. A's number equals the shared turn value (0), so A enters while B and C spin. When A unlocks, turn is incremented to 1, so B (whose number is 1) goes in next, then C.

evidence.quote: One final hardware primitive is the fetch-and-add instruction, which atomically increments a value while returning the old value at a particular address.
when a thread wishes to acquire a lock, it first does an atomic fetch-and-add on the ticket value; that value is now considered this thread’s “turn” (myturn).
Unlock is accomplished simply by incrementing the turn such that the next waiting thread (if there is one) can now enter the critical section.
The globally shared lock->turn is then used to determine which thread’s turn it is; when (myturn == turn) for a given thread, it is that thread’s turn to enter the critical section.

input: what does futex wait do if the value isnt what you passed in, and what does wake do
expected_output: futex wait(address, expected) puts the calling thread to sleep, assuming the value at address equals expected. If the value is not equal, the call returns immediately. futex wake(address) wakes one thread that is waiting on the queue.

evidence.quote: The call to futex wait(address, expected) puts the calling thread to sleep, assuming the value at address is equal to expected. If it is not equal, the call returns immediately.
The call to the routine futex wake(address) wakes one thread that is waiting on the queue.

input: spinning locks keep checking nonstop so every waiting thread is guaranteed to get in eventually, right?
expected_output: No. Spin locks don't provide any fairness guarantees. A spinning thread may spin forever under contention, so spin locks are not fair and may lead to starvation.

evidence.quote: spin locks don’t provide any fairness guarantees. Indeed, a thread spinning may spin forever, under contention. Spin locks are not fair and may lead to starvation.

input: so the lock that puts waiters to sleep has no spinning at all right?
expected_output: Not quite. The guard acts as a spin-lock around the flag and queue manipulations, so the approach doesn't avoid spin-waiting entirely. However, the time spent spinning is quite limited, just a few instructions inside the lock and unlock code instead of the user-defined critical section.

evidence.quote: basically as a spin-lock around the flag and queue manipulations the lock is using. This approach thus doesn’t avoid spin-waiting entirely;
However, the time spent spinning is quite limited (just a few instructions inside the lock and unlock code, instead of the user-defined critical section), and thus this approach may be reasonable.

input: In a lock built from sleep and wake calls, what can go wrong if a thread is switched out right before it goes to sleep and the holder releases the lock meanwhile, and how does Solaris prevent it?
expected_output: The waiting thread's later park would sleep forever (potentially), because the wakeup happened before it slept. This is the wakeup/waiting race. Solaris adds setpark(): the thread indicates it is about to park, and if another thread calls unpark before park is actually called, the subsequent park returns immediately instead of sleeping.

evidence.quote: A switch at that time to another thread (say, a thread holding the lock) could lead to trouble, for example, if that thread then released the lock. The subsequent park by the first thread would then sleep forever (potentially).
If it then happens to be interrupted and another thread calls unpark before park is actually called, the subsequent park returns immediately instead of sleeping.
This problem is sometimes called the wakeup/waiting race; to avoid it, we need to do some extra work.
Solaris solves this problem by adding a third system call: setpark(). By calling this routine, a thread can indicate it is about to park.

input: if switching interrupts off is so bad for locks, is there anywhere it's still ok to use?
expected_output: Yes, inside the operating system itself. The OS can use interrupt masking to guarantee atomicity when accessing its own data structures, or to prevent certain messy interrupt handling situations. This makes sense because the trust issue disappears inside the OS, which always trusts itself to perform privileged operations.

evidence.quote: operating system itself will use interrupt masking to guarantee atomicity when accessing its own data structures, or at least to prevent certain messy interrupt handling situations from arising.
This usage makes sense, as the trust issue disappears inside the OS, which always trusts itself to perform privileged operations anyhow.
